## Results

Between March 01, 2020, and Septembre 30, 2024, n = 385 individulas who committed sexual offenses against children have been screened for eligibility, of whom 16 have not been randomized. N = 369 individuals were randomly assigned, n = 182 to the placebo arm and n = 187 to the intervention arm. N = 213 participants have been included in the ITT sample (n = 107 [57.22%] in the intervention arm and n = 106 [58.24%] in the placebo arm; see @fig-diagram-consort-flowchart). 

![Trial profile. ITT = Intention-to-treat.](resources/figures/diagram_consort_flowchart.png){#fig-diagram-consort-flowchart width=100%}

N = 99 participants finished the WBI, n = 44 (30.20%) in the intervention arm and n = 55 (22.40%) in the placebo arm. Two female participants were randomized. The trial was closed at Septembre 30, 2024 before all participants have been able to finish the web-based intervention (n = 70 [56%], n = 39 [59%] in the intervention arm and n = 31 [53%] in the placebo arm).
Participants of both trial arms had been advised to work on each session within seven days, on each module within 28 days and to finish the HBI within 164 days. Participants needed more time finishing the WBI as adivised (see Supplementary material section "Protocl deviations"). 

::: {.callout-important}
Nur eines von beiden berichten:

Time required to complete the HBI modules was analysed using a mixed model for repeated measures and complemented by prespecified pairwise comparisons between treatment groups at each module. The MMRM estimated a mean completion time of 87 days at the reference condition (β = 87, 95% CI 69–105; p < 0·0001). There was evidence of timepoint–treatment interaction for Module 1 (post) (β = 27, 95% CI 1·5–53; p = 0·038), Module 3 (β = 26, 3·4–49; p = 0·025), and Module 4 (β = 32, 11–52; p = 0·0030), indicating longer completion times in the intervention group compared with placebo at these modules. No interaction effects were observed for Modules 2, 5, or 6 (all p > 0·05).Consistent with the MMRM results, pairwise comparisons showed numerically longer completion times in the intervention group across all modules, with the largest group differences observed for Modules 1, 3, and 4. For Module 4, the unadjusted comparison indicated a statistically significant difference between groups (mean 73 days [SD 60] vs 51 days [35]; p = 0·021), although this difference did not remain significant after Holm–Bonferroni adjustment (q = 0·13). For Modules 1 and 3, differences were of similar magnitude but narrowly missed conventional statistical significance (Module 1: p = 0·053; Module 3: p = 0·055). No evidence of group differences was found for Modules 2, 5, or 6 in pairwise analyses (all adjusted q > 0·99). Across both analyses, completion time decreased over successive modules irrespective of treatment allocation. In the MMRM, significant reductions in completion time were observed for Modules 2, 4, 5, and 6 compared with Module 1, with the largest decrease at Module 6 (β = −45, −65 to −24; p < 0·0001). Increasing amounts of missing data were observed at later modules in both groups. Overall, the MMRM and pairwise analyses were concordant, suggesting that participants generally completed later HBI modules more quickly, while the intervention was associated with longer engagement time for selected modules—most notably Module 4—although pairwise effects were attenuated after adjustment for multiple comparisons.

Cumulative time from the start of Module 1 to completion of each subsequent HBI module was analysed using a mixed model for repeated measures and complemented by pairwise group comparisons. The MMRM estimated a mean time to complete Module 1 of 87 days at the reference condition (β = 87, 95% CI 69–105; p < 0·0001).
There was strong evidence of a timepoint–treatment interaction across all modules, with participants in the intervention group requiring significantly more cumulative time to complete the programme than those in the placebo group. The magnitude of the group difference increased progressively over time (Module 1: β = 27, 95% CI 1·9–53; p = 0·035; Module 2: β = 44, 3·3–85; p = 0·034; Module 3: β = 77, 13–141; p = 0·019; Module 4: β = 113, 30–195; p = 0·0078; Module 5: β = 126, 30–223; p = 0·011; Module 6: β = 132, 29–236; p = 0·013).
Consistent with these model‑based estimates, pairwise comparisons showed numerically longer cumulative completion times in the intervention group at all modules. Unadjusted analyses indicated statistically significant group differences at Module 4 (mean 260 days [SD 138] vs 223 days [122]; p = 0·048) and Module 5 (325 [161] vs 258 [113]; p = 0·028), whereas differences at Modules 1, 2, 3, and 6 did not reach statistical significance (all p ≥ 0·053). After adjustment for multiple comparisons using the Holm–Bonferroni method, none of the pairwise differences remained statistically significant (all q ≥ 0·17).
Independent of treatment allocation, cumulative completion time increased substantially with each successive module (all p < 0·0001), rising from an additional 69 days at Module 2 (β = 69, 55–83) to 333 days at Module 6 (β = 333, 273–393) compared with Module 1.
Overall, both analyses indicate that total time to complete the HBI programme increased steadily over the course of the intervention and was consistently longer in the intervention group, with evidence of increasing divergence between groups over time in the MMRM, although pairwise differences were attenuated after correction for multiple testing.
:::

### Baseline characteristics

[@tbl-baseline-characteristics] shows sociodemographic, criminological and mental health baseline characteristics (see Supplementary material pp. XXX for all assessed baseline characteristics). 

{{< include _includes/tbl_baseline_characteristics.qmd >}}

With regard to strata, only n = 89 (40%) participants were mixed offenders (at least one conviction §176 ff StGB; n = 44 [41%] in the intervention arm and n = 45 [40%] in the placebo arm) and n = 132 (60%) were hands-off offenders (only convictions based on $184b StGB; n = 64 [59%] in the intervention arm and n = 68 [60%] in the placebo arm). The majority of  participants (n = 176 [80%]) were under community supervision (Bewährungshilfe §§56, 57 StGB; n = 88 [81%] in the intervention arm and n = 88 [78%] in the placebo arm). Only n = 45 (20%) have been under post-release supervision (Führungsaufsicht §§68 ff StGB; n = 20 [19%] in the intervention arm and n = 25 [22%] in the placebo arm). N = 70 (32%) of the ITT sample had additional external treatment in addition to community supervision as usual (n = 33 [31%] in the intervention arm and n = 37 [33%] in the placebo arm), n = 151 (68%) had no additional treatment (n = 75 [69%] in the intervention arm and n = 76 [67%] in the placebo arm). The majority of participants (n = 180 [81%]) had a low static risk to re-offend at baseline (n = 87 [81%] in the intervention arm and n = 93 [82%] in the placebo arm). N = 41 (19%) had a low-medium, medium-high or high risk to re-offend (n = 21 [19%] in the intervention arm and n = 20 [18%] in the placebo arm).

Overall, n = 70 (32%) received an external in-face treatment during participation (psychotherapy and/or medical treatment), but the court ordered this for n = 124 (56%). Only n = 48 (38.71%) of all participants who have an ordered treatment also in fact received external treatment at enrolement, the majority (n = 76; 61.29%) not.

All participants (n = 213 [100%]) had the German nationality, data on ethnicity has not been assessed.

### Harms

The interim analysis provided no evidence for the necessity to stopp the trial. During trial, no safety concerns were raised by researchers involved in the programme and no events were reported to the sponsor or ethics committee. Furthermore, wether supervision officer nor online coaches reported hints to recidivism or concrete preparation for recidivism in in-app messages or during working on guided exercises. 

::: {.callout-important}
Das lassen wir besser weg und wir nehmen nur die Tabelle!

Kaplan–Meier survival curves for time to first recidivism event (as reported by supervision officers in the EQ) indicated a very low incidence of recidivism in both study arms during the first year after initiation of module 1 [see @fig-kaplan-meyer-recidivism]. After 12 months, the estimated proportion of participants without recidivism was 1.00 (95% CI [0.94, 1.00]) in the intervention group (n = 108) and 0.98 (95% CI [0.88, 1.00]) in the placebo group (n = 113). Two recidivism events were observed in the placebo group, whereas no events occurred in the intervention group. A substantial proportion of participants were censored prior to the 12-month follow-up (47% in the intervention group, 66% in the placebo group; see [@tbl-difference-proportion]). The between-group comparison of the proportions without recidivism at one year (placebo minus intervention arm) yielded a difference of –0.022 (95% CI [–0.12, 0.046]; p = .76), indicating no statistically significant effect of the intervention compared to placebo (see [@tbl-proportion-without-recidivism]).
:::

Overall, adverse events as assessed with the MRQ, were rare. Indicators of contact‑related risk (contact planning or preparation) and urges related to CSA or consumption of CSEM were not reported by any participant in either group. Other risk‑related outcomes, including elevated sexual tension, impaired control over sexual thoughts and behaviour, and suicidal ideation, were reported by ≤1·9% of participants in each group, with no meaningful differences between the intervention and placebo groups. Higher frequencies were observed for measures of general psychological distress. Feeling unable to cope with mental burden was reported by 4·1% of participants overall (6·5% in the intervention group vs 1·8% in the placebo group). A current mental crisis was reported by 6·8% (10% vs 3·5%), and very poor current mood by 5·4% (7·4% vs 3·5%). However, none of these group differences were statistically significant in unadjusted analyses or after Holm correction for multiple testing (all q ≥ 0·44). Overall, there was no evidence that participation in the WBI was associated with an increased frequency of severe or risk‑related adverse events compared with placebo.

### Main outcome
The mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) for the CARES total score showed no evidence of a treatment effect over time, with no significant timepoint × treatment interaction at any module (all p ≥ 0·149; table X). 

{{< include _includes/tbl_prim_CARES_mmrm.qmd >}}

Sensitivity analysis revealed no different results (all p ≥ 0·169; see supplementary materials table XX). An exploratory MMRM additionally adjusting for time since the beginning of module one yielded consistent results, with no significant timepoint × treatment interaction (all p ≥ 0·293; see supplementary table X). The analysis of the primary endpoint as originally specified in the statistical analysis plan yielded consistent findings, with no significant timepoint × treatment interaction in the MMRM (all p ≥ 0·588; see supplementary section “IoD”).
Exploratory pairwise comparisons of change from baseline between treatment groups indicated a statistical trend at module 2 (p = 0·051; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·31). At this timepoint, the mean change from baseline was smaller in the intervention group (−0·3 [SD 3·9]) than in the placebo group (1·0 [5·5]). No other pairwise comparisons showed evidence of group differences (all p ≥ 0·53; supplementary table X).
Exploratory within‑group pre–post comparisons showed a significant reduction in CARES from pre‑ to post‑module one in the intervention group (t = −2·85, p = 0·0050; Holm‑Bonferroni q = 0·030; estimated relative effect p̂ = 0·451, 95% CI 0·417–0·485), with mean scores decreasing from 14 (SD 8) to 12 (9). No significant changes were observed at later modules (all p ≥ 0·15; supplementary table X).
Similarly, in the placebo group, CARES decreased significantly from pre to post at module one (t = −3·88, p < 0·0001; q < 0·0001; p̂ = 0·428, 95% CI 0·392–0·465), with mean scores declining from 12 (8 SD) to 11 (9 SD). Two modules showed nominal pre–post differences that did not remain significant after adjustment for multiple testing: module two (p = 0·050, q = 0·24) and module 3 (p = 0·047, q = 0·24), suggesting a decrease. All other modules showed no evidence of change (all p ≥ 0·54; supplementary table X).

### Secondary outcomes

[@tbl-sec-pairwise-intervention] shows descriptive statistics and the results of pairwise pre–post comparisons for each secondary endpoint in the intervention group, [@tbl-sec-pairwise-placebo] for the placebo arm. 

{{< include _includes/tbl_sec_pairwise_intervention.qmd >}}

Three measures showed statistically significant pre–post differences in the intervention arm. The CVTRQ total score increased from 84 (SD 7) at baseline to 86 (8) at post‑measurement (p = 0·0060; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·078), indicating improved treatment readiness. The DERS impulsivity subscale score increased from 6·24 (SD 2·26) to 6·72 (2·25; p = 0·0050; q = 0·070), suggesting increased impulsivity‑related difficulties. By contrast, the ESIQ total score decreased from 90 (SD 12) to 87 (12; p = 0·0010; q = 0·015), indicating a reduction in explicit sexual interests. One measure reached nominal significance but did not survive adjustment for multiple testing: the SSIC score increased slightly from 26·5 (SD 4·6) to 27·1 (4·3; p = 0·049; q = 0·59), suggesting a possible, but not statistically robust, increase in perceived self‑efficacy. The SOI‑R subscale score decreased from 11 (20 SD) to 9 (21; p = 0·071; q = 0·79), indicating a potential reduction in desire for sexual activity with children, although this change did not reach statistical significance after adjustment. Several additional measures showed statistical trends. The UCLA total score decreased from 28·5 (SD 3·9) to 28·0 (4·1; p = 0·066; q = 0·73), suggesting a possible reduction in loneliness. The OQMPR score decreased from 29 (SD 9) to 28 (9; p = 0·084; q = 0·84), indicating a potential reduction in psychological reactance. All other measures, including RCQ, F‑Soz‑U, BIS‑15, CUSI, NARQ (externalising strategies), SPSI‑R, BMS, EKK‑R, and HBI‑19, showed no significant pre–post differences (all p ≥ 0·13).

{{< include _includes/tbl_sec_pairwise_placebo.qmd >}}

In the placebo group, only one measure showed a statistically significant pre–post difference. The F‑Soz‑U total score increased from 3·74 (SD 0·84) at baseline to 3·88 (SD 0·89) at post‑measurement (p = 0·0030; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·045), indicating improved perceived social support. No additional measures reached nominal significance (unadjusted p < 0·05), and no outcomes showed statistical trends. All other measures, including CVTRQ, RCQ, OQMPR, UCLA, BIS‑15, CUSI, DERS impulsivity, NARQ (externalising strategies), SPSI‑R, BMS, ESIQ, SOI‑R, SSIC, EKK‑R, and HBI‑19, showed no significant pre–post differences (all p ≥ 0·12).

Exploratory analyses of change from baseline in secondary endpoints identified two questionnaires with statistically significant differences between the intervention and placebo groups (table X). The ESIQ total score decreased in the intervention group (−3·6 [SD 5·4]) but remained largely unchanged in the placebo group (−0·1 [7·9]; p = 0·0020; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·030), indicating a statistically significant reduction in explicit sexual interests confined to the intervention group.
Change from baseline in the DERS impulsivity subscale was greater in the intervention group (0·49 [SD 2·10]) than in the placebo group (−0·15 [1·24]; p = 0·024; q = 0·34), representing a nominal, but not statistically robust, increase in impulsivity‑related difficulties in the intervention group and a decrease in the placebo group during module 3.
One additional questionnaire showed a statistical trend: the SSIC change‑from‑baseline score was slightly higher in the intervention group (0·6 [SD 3·6]) than in the placebo group (0·1 [4·5]; p = 0·077; q > 0·99), suggesting a possible, though statistically unsupported, improvement in perceived self‑efficacy in reducing sexual interest in children.
All other measures, including CVTRQ, RCQ, F‑Soz‑U, OQMPR, UCLA, BIS‑15, CUSI, NARQ (externalising strategies), SPSI‑R, BMS, EKK‑R, SOI‑R, and HBI‑19, showed no evidence of differences between groups (all p ≥ 0·14; table X).

### Ancillary outcomes

The mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) for the WHO‑5 total score showed no evidence of group differences over time, with no significant timepoint × treatment interaction at any assessment (all p ≥ 0·11; table X). The estimated intervention effects relative to placebo were 1·7 at module 1 (post), −1·8 at module 2 (pre), −1·6 at module 2 (post), −0·86 at module 3 (pre), −4·5 at module 3 (post), 0·10 at module 4 (pre), −4·3 at module 4 (post), −2·4 at module 5 (pre), −2·9 at module 5 (post), −1·9 at module 6 (pre), and −0·15 at module 6 (post). No significant effects were observed for additional treatment (β = 0·25; p = 0·91), type of supervision (β = −2·9; p = 0·29), or offence type (hands‑on vs hands‑off; β = 1·9; p = 0·40). Baseline static recidivism risk showed a non‑significant negative association with WHO‑5 scores (β = −0·94; p = 0·30). By contrast, baseline WHO‑5 score was strongly and positively associated with subsequent WHO‑5 outcomes (β = 0·68; p < 0·0001).
With respect to timepoint main effects, none of the modules differed significantly from module 1 (post; all p ≥ 0·24).

The mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) analysing the WAI‑SR COACH showed significant timepoint × treatment interaction effects at several post‑module assessments (table X). Compared with placebo, model‑based estimates for the intervention group were 2·4 at module 2 (post; p = 0·025), 3·8 at module 3 (post; p = 0·0044), 3·4 at module 4 (post; p = 0·0067), 2·1 at module 5 (post; p = 0·13), and 4·3 at module 6 (post; p = 0·0051). Pairwise pre–post comparisons within the intervention group showed statistically significant increases in coach‑rated WAI‑SR scores at module 2 (post), increasing from 42 (SD 11) to 44 (SD 9; p = 0·0020; Holm‑adjusted q = 0·010), and at module 6 (post), increasing from 46 (SD 11) to 49 (SD 9; p = 0·0040; q = 0·016). No other modules in the intervention group showed significant pre–post changes (all q ≥ 0·62). In the placebo group, no significant pre–post changes were observed at any module (all q > 0·99; tables X). Exploratory analyses of change scores between treatment groups identified two timepoints with nominal group differences (table Z). Change from module 1 (pre) to module 2 (post) was greater in the intervention group (median 3 [Q1 −2, Q3 8]) than in the placebo group (1 [−3, 5]; p = 0·025; q = 0·13). Similarly, change from module 5 (post) to module 6 (post) was greater in the intervention group (2 [0, 6]) than in the placebo group (0 [−2, 4]; p = 0·036; q = 0·14). No other difference scores showed evidence of group differences (all q ≥ 0·18).

The mixed model for repeated measures (MMRM) for the supervisor‑rated WAI‑SR SUPERVISOR showed significant timepoint × treatment interaction effects at several post‑module assessments, indicating higher working‑alliance ratings in the intervention group compared with placebo (table X). Significant between‑group differences were observed at modules 2, 3, 4, and 6 (post), with a nominal effect at module 5. No significant effects were found for additional treatment, type of supervision, offence type, or baseline static recidivism risk, whereas baseline WAI‑SR score was strongly and positively associated with subsequent scores (p < 0·0001). No overall time effects were observed relative to module 2 (post).
Pairwise pre–post comparisons showed a significant increase in supervisor‑rated WAI‑SR scores within the intervention group at module 2 (post), with a smaller, nominally significant increase at module 6 that did not survive adjustment for multiple testing. No significant pre–post changes were observed in the placebo group at any module.
Exploratory between‑group analyses of change scores supported these findings, showing a significantly greater improvement from module 1 (pre) to module 2 (post) in the intervention group compared with placebo, and a trend towards a greater improvement from module 5 to module 6. No other between‑group differences were observed.
Overall, improvements in supervisor‑rated working alliance were concentrated in the intervention group, particularly at an early stage of the programme, with weaker and non‑robust effects at later modules.
